title: The crusades, honestly
hookLine: armed pilgrimages that killed Muslims, Jews and Eastern Christians; crusaders sacked Constantinople; later popes apologized

cards: "God wills it." One chronicler says that's what a crowd shouted back at a pope in an open field at Clermont, in France. The pope was Urban.
The versions of his speech that reached us were written down afterward, and they don't agree word for word.

But between them they carry the call: Christians in the East need help, and, in most versions, Jerusalem is the goal. Men sewed crosses onto their clothes and set out. Others followed in later expeditions.
That's the beginning of what we now call the crusades, and today we tell it honestly.

teach.b: Honestly means holding more than one thing. Some who went believed they were doing penance, leaving home to walk toward the city where Jesus died. And the armies did terrible things.
On the way east, crusading bands attacked Jewish communities in the Rhineland; Jewish chroniclers wrote down the names and the grief.
When Jerusalem fell, crusader writers themselves described the killing of the city's Muslims, and wrote of it as triumph; other sources tell of its Jews killed too.
In a later crusade, armies that had set out for the East turned on Constantinople, a Christian city, and sacked it, churches and all.
A Byzantine historian who lived through it, Niketas Choniates, wrote that these men who carried the cross on their shoulders showed less mercy than the Saracens, the name then used for Muslims.
The pope of the day, Innocent the third, wrote angrily against what was done. Set all that beside the Gospel.

When one of his followers drew a sword in the garden, Jesus told him, in Matthew's King James words: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword."
Much later, the churches looked back. At a Day of Pardon, Pope John Paul the second asked forgiveness for violence some Christians had used in the service of truth.
Speaking in Athens, he said the sack of Constantinople fills Catholics with deep regret. Historians still argue over motives, and different churches tell the story with different weight.

how: Churches remember the crusades in different ways; the Catholic Church has asked forgiveness for violence done by its members, and some Christians take part in services of repentance and in work for reconciliation with Jews, Muslims and Orthodox Christians.

games.why: John Paul the second said the sack fills Catholics with deep regret. today's line comes out of that looking back.

practice: Bring to mind people harmed by violence done in God's name: Jewish families in the Rhineland, the Muslims and Jews of Jerusalem, Christians in Constantinople, and people in our own time, of any faith or none.
If you pray, pray for them, and for those who carry the memory; if you don't, hold them in silence. Then, gently, ask where faith has ever been used as a weapon in your own life, even with words.

wordCard.voice: Crusade. The armed pilgrimages called by popes and marked with a cross on the clothes, remembered now with honesty and with sorrow.

carryVoice: Your line: never again in his name. Honest memory is where that begins. Rest well.
